   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?

   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?

Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Comcast fits few Rule Breaker traits: it is the incumbent in mature cable and media markets, not the top dog of an emerging industry, and the stock has fallen about 24% over the past year and about 46% over five years on a dividend-adjusted basis. Its brands (Xfinity, NBC, Universal, Peacock) are well known but not loved, and commentators call the stock cheap rather than overvalued.
summaries.buffett: Comcast has some Buffett-like traits: big, understandable franchises, heavy free cash flow ($19.2 billion in 2025) and steady buybacks that cut diluted shares from 4,654 million in 2021 to 3,709 million in 2025. But its broadband moat is eroding, it carries $87.4 billion of debt, returns on capital are only around 8%, and retained earnings have not produced share-price gains, so it looks more like a cheap, challenged business than a wonderful one.
summaries.munger: Inverting, there are clear ways Comcast could keep shrinking in value: fiber and fixed wireless taking broadband customers, cord-cutting, rising sports costs and leverage. At about 7 times earnings the price reflects much of this, but Munger preferred great businesses at fair prices over fair businesses at cheap prices, and Comcast's quality is declining.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would see Comcast as a slow grower or asset play with a possible catalyst in the planned NBCUniversal/Sky spin-off; the P/E of about 7 looks cheap, but earnings are not growing (2026 consensus EPS $3.50, down from $4.31 adjusted in 2025), so the PEG test fails. The story is easy to explain but the trend in the core business is down.
summaries.fisher: Comcast keeps launching products (Xfinity Mobile with 9.3 million lines, Peacock with 48 million paid subscribers, Epic Universe), but it is not an R&D-driven company with a long runway of above-average sales growth. Management is long-tenured and capable at deals, yet sales are flat and margins have not expanded, so it scores poorly on Fisher's growth points.
summaries.graham: On Graham's defensive-investor numbers Comcast looks attractive: a large company profitable every year for at least a decade, EPS up from $1.62 (split-adjusted) in 2015 to $5.39 in 2025, a P/E of about 7 and P/E times P/B of about 6. It fails the 20-year dividend record (dividends began in 2008) and its current ratio of 0.82 and heavy debt fall short of Graham's balance-sheet standards.
summaries.thiel: Comcast is not a Zero to One company: it has no 10x proprietary technology, operates in competitive, mature markets and is losing share to fiber and wireless rivals. Its strengths are distribution and scale, but its position in 10-20 years looks weaker, not stronger.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price with management focused on efficiency; Comcast is cheap (about 22% FCF yield on company-defined free cash flow) and is restructuring, but revenue is shrinking and it is not a beneficiary of the AI platform shift. It is more a value or special-situation story than a compounding growth story.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller wants accelerating earnings and rising estimates; Comcast has the opposite, with 2026 EPS expected to fall about 19% and broadband losses continuing. The upcoming NBCUniversal/Sky separation is a catalyst, but the trend and price momentum are negative.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith seeks high returns on capital with little debt and organic growth; Comcast earns about 8% returns, relies on $87.4 billion of debt and has flat revenue, so it does not fit despite its low valuation.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Comcast scores well on earnings yield (LTM operating income of about $18.1 billion is about 11% of its roughly $158 billion enterprise value) but only moderately on return on capital given its huge asset base. It could appear in a Magic Formula screen as a cheap stock rather than a high-return one.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented and honest managers, and a long reinvestment runway; Comcast's business is under competitive pressure, its dual-class structure gives the Roberts family a third of the votes, and it has few high-return reinvestment opportunities, so it fits poorly.
summaries.pabrai: Comcast offers a Dhandho-style setup in part: low valuation (P/E about 7), strong free cash flow and a catalyst in the business split, limiting downside. But its problems in broadband are structural rather than temporary, and leverage adds risk, so the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' case is only partial.
summaries.wood: Comcast is not an ARK-style disruptive innovator; it is an incumbent being disrupted by streaming, fiber and wireless, with no leading role in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics.
summaries.ackman: Ackman likes simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and a catalyst; Comcast's spin-offs (Versant in January 2026, NBCUniversal/Sky planned about mid-2027) and low valuation could appeal, but its predictability has weakened and its leverage and competitive pressure fall short of his quality bar.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economies-shared businesses that pass savings to customers; Comcast instead raised prices for years and is now losing customers, so it does not fit the Nomad model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with great technology; Comcast is a 1963-founded incumbent in mature markets, so it falls outside his approach.
summaries.nash: On Tom Nash's checks Comcast fails most of the hard filters: revenue is not growing 10% a year, debt ($87.4 billion) far exceeds cash ($7.6 billion), operating margin (about 15% over the last twelve months) is below 20%, and it has a co-CEO structure. Its strengths are cheapness, cash flow and consistent earnings beats, but it scores about 45 on his 13-category scale.

momentum.evidence: CMCSA closed at $22.05 on Oct 26, 2026, down 24.39% over 52 weeks (StockAnalysis), while the S&P 500 rose.

g4.evidence: Comcast is run by long-time Chairman Brian Roberts and co-CEO Mike Cavanagh and is about 90% institutionally owned, but it has no famous investor or partner championing it.

g6.evidence: Commentators generally call Comcast cheap (trailing P/E about 7, forward P/E 6.44) rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: Its businesses (cable broadband, TV networks, studios, parks) are understandable, but the ongoing Versant spin-off, Sky Germany sale and planned NBCUniversal/Sky separation make the picture complicated.

b2.evidence: Comcast has been profitable every year with revenue rising from $103,564M in 2020 to $123,707M in 2025, but operating income swung from $14,041M (2022) to $23,314M (2023) and is falling in 2026.

integrity.evidence: Management returned $11.7 billion to shareholders in 2025 and reports candidly, but the Roberts family's Class B shares carry one-third of the votes and the 2018 Sky deal led to an $8.6 billion impairment in 2022.

b6.evidence: Comcast built its empire through large acquisitions (NBCUniversal, Sky), but it is now simplifying by spinning off Versant and planning to separate NBCUniversal and Sky.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 8% (StockAnalysis) and the company relies on $87.4 billion of debt.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $19,235M in 2025 (company definition), close to net income of $19,998M that included a $7.1 billion after-tax Hulu gain, and $12,716M in the first nine months of 2026.

b10.evidence: Despite retaining and reinvesting billions, the dividend-adjusted share price fell from about $41 in October 2021 to $22.05 in October 2026.

safety.evidence: At about 7 times trailing earnings and a simple DCF value near $25 per share the price is below a conservative value, but the margin of safety is modest given shrinking broadband and high debt.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E around 7, forward P/E of 6.44 and FCF yield over 20% are low for a business with stable cash flows, even with little growth.

mu5.evidence: Failure paths include accelerating broadband losses to fiber and fixed wireless, cord-cutting, sports cost inflation and leverage, but strong cash flow and diversified assets make outright failure unlikely.

reinvest.evidence: Returns on capital are around 8% and the core broadband and video businesses are shrinking, leaving few high-return reinvestment opportunities beyond parks and wireless.

ly2.evidence: It fits Lynch's slow grower or asset play category, with a simple story of cheap cash flows plus a spin-off catalyst, but the core trend is negative.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 7 exceeds expected earnings growth: 2026 EPS is forecast to fall 18.8% and 2027 EPS to rise only about 1%.

runway.evidence: Consensus sees revenue falling from $123.7 billion in 2025 to about $119.8 billion in 2026 and $116.6 billion in 2027.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 4,654 million in 2021 to 3,562 million in Q3 2026, but Comcast suspended buybacks from Q3 2026 and there is no sign of notable insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Comcast is covered by about 27 analysts and is widely followed, though out of favour.

fi2.evidence: It has added Xfinity Mobile (9.3 million lines at end-2025), Peacock (48 million paid subscribers) and Epic Universe as older products like pay TV decline.

fi3.evidence: Product spending has produced X1, Peacock and wireless growth, but it has not stopped broadband and video customer losses.

fi4.evidence: Comcast is a strong marketer and bundler (best-ever 1.5 million wireless line adds in 2025), but it still lost 144,000 broadband customers in Q3 2026.

longterm.evidence: Management invested in Epic Universe, Peacock and network upgrades for the long term, but also prioritised buybacks and dividends ($11.7 billion returned in 2025).

gr1.evidence: Comcast had $123.7 billion of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $78.5 billion.

ni10.evidence: Net income attributable to Comcast was positive in each of the last ten years, including $8,695M in 2016 and a low of $5,370M in 2022.

gr4.evidence: Comcast initiated its first quarterly dividend in 2008, so its record is about 18 years, short of 20.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.24 in 2015 ($1.62 after the 2017 two-for-one split) to $5.39 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: At $22.05 the price is about 5 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of $4.41.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 7.0 times P/B of about 0.85 is about 6, well under 22.5.

th1.evidence: Comcast's hybrid fiber-coax network is not 10x better than fiber or 5G rivals.

timing.evidence: Market timing is unfavourable for cable: fiber build-outs and fixed wireless are taking share and cord-cutting continues.

th3.evidence: Comcast is a large incumbent in mature markets, not a company that dominated a small niche and is expanding from there.

team.evidence: Brian Roberts has led Comcast since 2002 and built it into a global group, and Mike Cavanagh (former JPMorgan CFO) is co-CEO, but results and share performance have been weak.

th5.evidence: Comcast has deep distribution: a network passing more than 65 million homes and businesses, retail stores and bundling of broadband, mobile and TV.

durable.evidence: Its wired network and content assets will likely still matter in 10-20 years, but broadband share is being eroded by fiber and wireless and pay TV is in decline.

th7.evidence: Comcast is not pursuing an opportunity others have missed; its growth areas (wireless, streaming, parks) are crowded.

trend.evidence: Comcast is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud; its core broadband market is maturing.

dr1.evidence: 2026 EPS is forecast at $3.50, down 18.8% from $4.31 in 2025, with 2027 at $3.54.

dr2.evidence: The planned NBCUniversal/Sky separation (expected about mid-2027) could leave a cleaner connectivity company, but broadband losses may continue.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would help a company with $87.4 billion of debt, but a weak consumer and advertising market would hurt.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include the NBCUniversal/Sky spin-off, the sale of a retained stake of up to 19.9% in NBCUniversal and Peacock turning profitable ($261M EBITDA in Q3 2026).

dr7.evidence: Structural decline in broadband and video and high leverage make it hard to justify a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 72% if only programming and production costs ($34,951M in 2025) are counted, but much of the cost sits in other operating expenses and operating margin is only 16.7%.

fcfyield.evidence: LTM free cash flow of about $17.1 billion (2025 $19,235M less 9M 2025 $14,866M plus 9M 2026 $12,716M) is about 22% of the $78.5 billion market value.

gb2.evidence: LTM operating income of about $18.1 billion is about 11% of an enterprise value of roughly $158 billion.

pa2.evidence: Some pressures are temporary (Versant and Sky Germany deconsolidation, NBA start-up costs), but broadband competition from fiber and wireless is structural.

pa4.evidence: Strong cash flow and a low valuation limit the chance of permanent loss, but $87.4 billion of debt and shrinking customers add risk.

wo1.evidence: Comcast is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its costs are not falling quickly with volume; programming and network costs keep rising.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable markets (US broadband, pay TV, media) will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: It is largely insulated from commodity prices, but its heavy debt makes it sensitive to interest rates and its advertising and parks revenue to the economy.

ns1.evidence: Comcast has historically raised prices rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Its position in 10-20 years is unlikely to be clearly stronger given fiber and wireless competition.

va2.evidence: Broadband solves an essential need for internet access, but it is a commodity many rivals also provide.

tn1.evidence: Comcast is an old cable and media business, not one built for a secular trend like AI or energy.

tn2.evidence: The market prices it as a declining cable company; after the NBCUniversal/Sky split it will become a pure connectivity company, which may or may not be re-rated.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company outside Nash's avoid zones (not small cap, Chinese, commodity, airline, seasonal or startup).

tn4.evidence: It is profitable, but revenue has been flat (2025 $123,707M vs 2024 $123,731M) and debt of $87.4 billion far exceeds cash of $7.6 billion.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive every recent quarter ($4,211M in Q3 2026), but debt has exceeded cash in every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue was flat in 2025 and consensus expects a 3.2% decline in 2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about -0.6% (LTM) plus an FCF margin of about 14% is about 13, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue fell $24M while total costs and expenses rose from $100,434M to $103,035M.

tn9.evidence: It triggers several instant kills: more debt than cash, operating margin below 20% (16.7% in 2025) and revenue growth below 10% and falling.

tn10.evidence: No major legal threat is evident, but the planned separation needs regulatory approvals and media ownership faces political scrutiny.

tn11.evidence: Comcast provides broadband, mobile, TV and entertainment that help households and businesses stay connected and entertained, charging monthly subscriptions plus advertising, licensing fees and park tickets.

tn13.evidence: Total about 45: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5 (about 15% LTM), short interest 10 (about 2%), institutional ownership 10 (about 90%), revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture and mission 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue did not grow every year (2025 was slightly down), operating margin did not expand (16.9% in 2020 vs 16.7% in 2025) and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage was about 4.7x in 2025 (operating income $20,672M / interest $4,409M), but the current ratio is 0.82 and assets excluding goodwill ($204.5 billion) are only about 1.2x liabilities ($165.1 billion) at Sep 30, 2026.

tn18.evidence: Brian Roberts has 20+ years as CEO and controls one-third of the votes, but he is not the founder, has no known open-market purchases and recent execution has been mixed.

tn20.evidence: Comcast beat adjusted EPS estimates in each of the last four quarters by about 8-11% (Q3 2026: $1.07 vs $0.99).

tn21.evidence: It has a co-CEO structure (Roberts and Cavanagh) and declining operating margins, both on Nash's red-flag list.

tn22.evidence: Comcast has large revenue, solid fundamentals and has been shrinking its share count, not issuing shares.

tn24.evidence: At $22.05 a 12% DCF with a 12.1% FCF margin implies revenue shrinking about 0.8% a year, slightly below recent flat results but close to 2026-27 consensus declines.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year averages (0.6% revenue growth, 12.1% FCF margin), 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, the value is about $24.8 per share versus $22.05.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of 6.44 is low versus peers, but with EPS expected to fall in 2026 and grow about 1% in 2027 the PEG is well above 1.
